title: The King Returns: Mercy, Rewards, and a Divided People
summary: David's grief for Absalom turns the army's victory into shame until Joab bluntly warns him that he will lose his men, and David goes out to sit in the gate. The tribes debate bringing the king back; David wins Judah by appealing to kinship and by promising Absalom's commander Amasa Joab's post. At the Jordan he spares Shimei, hears Mephibosheth's side of Ziba's story and divides the land between them, and says farewell to the aged Barzillai. The chapter ends with Israel and Judah quarreling over who has the greater claim on the king.
story: Absalom is dead, but the kingdom is not yet healed. This chapter reverses David's flight in chapters 15-16. The people he met on the way out meet him again on the way back: Shimei, who cursed him; Ziba and Mephibosheth, whose stories conflict; and Barzillai, who fed him at Mahanaim. Each meeting shows something of the restored king. But underneath the return lies a fault line. The rivalry between Judah and the northern tribes (called Israel here) breaks into the open in verses 41-43 and leads directly to Sheba's revolt in chapter 20. That same fault line will split the kingdom in two after Solomon's death (1 Kings 12).
historical:
David's kingdom joined two groups that had never fully merged. Judah had made him king at Hebron first (2:4), and the northern tribes came to him seven years later (5:1-3). Absalom's revolt drew support from both, and now each must decide whether to bring David back. David's strategy is political. He works through the priests Zadok and Abiathar to shame the elders of Judah into acting first, and he offers Amasa, Absalom's commander and his own nephew, the command of the army in place of Joab. This wins over Absalom's former supporters, but it also humiliates Joab, and chapter 20 shows the result.

Gilgal, near Jericho, was a place of deep memory: Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan under Joshua (Joshua 4-5) and the place where Saul's kingship was renewed (1 Samuel 11:14-15). Crossing the Jordan at Gilgal made David's return a kind of second entry into the land. Barzillai's son (or relative) Chimham, who goes with David, may be remembered in the place name Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem (Jeremiah 41:17), and David later asks Solomon to show kindness to Barzillai's sons (1 Kings 2:7).
cultural:
Joab's rebuke turns on the public role of a king. Victory celebrations required the king to honor his soldiers; instead, David's mourning made them steal back into the city as if defeated. Sitting in the gate was where a king appeared to his people and heard their cases, so David's taking his seat there signals that he has resumed his role.

Mephibosheth's appearance tells its own story. He had not cared for his feet, trimmed his mustache, or washed his clothes since David left, the signs of mourning. That supports his claim that he had been loyal all along. Barzillai's reply (verses 34-37) shows how old age was spoken of: the loss of taste and hearing, and the desire to die near the tomb of one's parents. Family burial in the ancestral tomb mattered greatly. The quarrel at the end uses the image of shares: Israel claims ten shares in the king (ten tribes), while Judah claims closer kinship.
literary: The chapter is built as the mirror of David's flight. In chapters 15-16 David went down to the Jordan and met Ziba, Shimei, Hushai, and the Gileadites; now he comes back to the Jordan and meets Shimei, Ziba, Mephibosheth, and Barzillai. The key word is return (shuv), repeated through the chapter as the tribes debate returning the king. The verb cross over (avar) also recurs, eleven times, as the Jordan crossing becomes the stage for each encounter. The chapter begins with grief and ends with quarreling, and neither is resolved. David's words to Abishai, “Should any man be put to death in Israel today?” express the mood of amnesty he wants for his return, but the last verse, with Judah speaking “even harder” than Israel, shows that peace has not come.

outline.t: Joab rebukes David's grief, and the king sits in the gate
The tribes debate, and David wins Judah
Shimei begs for mercy and is spared
Mephibosheth's account and the division of the land
Israel and Judah quarrel over the king

doctrines.note: The restored king returns not by conquest but by the consent of the tribes, and his first acts are mercy (to Shimei) and reward (to Barzillai). The chapter shows kingship at its best and its fragile limits, as rival loyalties threaten to split the people.
Shimei says, “your servant knows that I have sinned.” His confession may be as much political as heartfelt, but David grants him life. Confession opens the door to mercy even when motives are mixed.

David faces a case (Ziba against Mephibosheth) where the truth cannot easily be known. His decision to divide the land has been read both as a wise compromise and as a failure of judgment, and the chapter invites reflection on justice under uncertainty.

words.note: Shuv, to return or turn back. The word dominates the chapter as the tribes ask why no one speaks of bringing the king back (verse 10) and Judah invites him to return (verse 14). The same verb is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, turning back to God.

Satan, adversary or opponent. David asks the sons of Zeruiah why they have become his adversaries today (verse 22). Here the word has its ordinary human meaning: someone who opposes or obstructs. Only later in the Old Testament does it become the title of the accuser, the Satan.

Mashiach, anointed one. Abishai wants Shimei executed because he cursed the LORD's anointed (verse 21). The king was God's anointed, set apart by anointing with oil; the same word, through Greek, gives us Messiah and Christ.
Chata, to sin. Shimei says, “your servant knows that I have sinned” (verse 20), echoing David's own confession to Nathan in 12:13. The confession gains him life.

christ: The chapter shows the anointed king (mashiach) returning to his people and meeting both enemies and friends with mercy and reward. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as the Messiah, the anointed son of David, who will return in glory. The Gospels also show him refusing to punish those who opposed him when he could have, as when he rebuked his disciples for wanting to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54-55). David's words to Abishai echo a kingly mercy that Jesus shows fully. The link is thematic rather than predictive; David's mercy is partial and politically calculated, and he later tells Solomon to deal with Shimei (1 Kings 2:8-9). The chapter points to a king whose mercy would be deeper and whose kingdom would not be divided.

hard.q: Who was telling the truth, Ziba or Mephibosheth?
hard.a: The text leaves this open, and readers disagree. Mephibosheth's appearance (unwashed and in mourning since David left), his explanation (Ziba took the donkeys and left him behind, and he was lame), and his willingness to let Ziba take everything all suggest he was loyal and that Ziba had lied to gain his master's property. Many interpreters conclude this. Others point out that Mephibosheth, as Saul's heir, had reason to hope for the kingdom's return to his family, and that his words could be a clever defense. David's decision to divide the land has been read as a wise compromise, as a tired king avoiding a hard judgment, or as a failure of justice toward a loyal man. The narrator does not settle it. What stands out is the contrast between Mephibosheth's words, “let Ziba take it all,” which value the king's return over property, and the way many others in the chapter are bargaining for advantage.

questions: Joab told David that his grief was costing him his people. When does private grief need to make room for public responsibility?
David spared Shimei on the day of his return. Why might mercy be especially fitting at a time of restoration?
Barzillai was content to go home and let a younger man receive the reward. What does his attitude teach about aging and generosity?
